name: Maya Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm on the ward-skills lab by nine, practising bed baths and taking blood pressure on plastic dummies, which is funnier than it sounds. Afternoons are anatomy lectures or the library, and Thursday evenings I help at a care home near my flat. I share the flat with two other nursing students, and we cook big pots of lentil stew on Sundays. My mum is a ward sister and a union rep, so I grew up hearing about short staffing at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise about not much, and that we should still teach people to do things by hand. At the care home they tried a scheduling app that mixed up two residents' medication times, so I've seen the hype wobble first-hand. Online I'd probably say nothing, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel relieved but a bit smug, which isn't a nice feeling. Nursing is hands-on and human, so a plateau means my plan stays the same. I'd still be scared of the ordinary stuff, like exams and whether I'm good enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: lectures, the skills lab, the care home on Thursdays. I'd apply for the summer healthcare assistant job at the hospital where my mum works, because it pays well and you learn faster on a real ward. I wouldn't change a thing about how I study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A quiet worry about staffing is always there, because hospitals were short of nurses long before AI. But my own place feels secure, and my family can cover everything if something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on as before. Is there anything about your degree that would still nag at you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the staffing. Even without AI there are never enough nurses, and I'll walk into that. A plateau doesn't fix the staffing, and that's the thing I'd actually be angry about, because my mum comes home exhausted every single week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your mum is a union rep. Would she be calm in that picture, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than she is at work, yes. She'd say the plateau gives unions more time to win proper staffing levels, and she'd probably be right. But she'd still be fighting the same fights she's fought for twenty years.

say: I'd say **AI hype** is mostly noise and that nursing still needs people.
I'd mention the care home scheduling app that **mixed up medication times**.
think: Privately I feel **relieved**, and a little smug about it.
My real fear is the **ordinary pressure** of staffing and exams, not AI.
do: Keep up lectures, the **skills lab** and Thursday evenings at the care home.
Apply for a **summer healthcare assistant job** at my mum's hospital.
feel: **Calm** about my place, with a steady worry about short staffing.
S0.quote: A plateau doesn't fix the staffing, and that's the thing I'd actually be angry about, because my mum comes home exhausted every single week.
fieldNote: She trusts what she has seen on a ward more than what she reads online.
Calm here comes from a **secure family** and a hands-on career, not from optimism.
Anger at **understaffing** appeared before AI was even raised.

steps.text: Keep attending skills-lab sessions and Thursday evenings at the care home
Apply for a summer healthcare assistant job on my mum's ward
Watch how the hospital's scheduling software performs before trusting it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules before the software arrives, not after. At the union meeting my mum took me to, a rep said every time a hospital buys a system, staff hear about it last. Online I'd share articles about nurses having a say, and I'd go to the student union meeting, which I've avoided so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm uneasy. Nursing is hands-on, so it should last longer than most jobs, but the paperwork half of it will get taken over fast. I worry the saved time won't go to patients, it'll go to cutting posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally learn what these tools actually do, probably by watching a friend use one, because I won't type my own essays into one. I'd join the student nurses' group that talks about workplace rights, and ask my mum for her old union handbook. I'd keep my grades high so I have choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like the ground is moving but I can still stand on it. I'm not afraid for my job, because bedside care is hard to swap. I'm afraid of a ward where nobody has time to talk to patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools at all. In this picture, does that become a problem for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really a problem yet, but it could become one. If every hospital team expects people to dictate notes into software, I'd be the awkward one. I'd rather be slow and sure than the nurse who clicks accept on something wrong, because a wrong dose doesn't care how fast the software was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of nursing do you think the software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The charting, the notes, the booking of beds and medicine orders. A nurse spends close to half a shift on that, my mum says. If software does it well, good, but someone has to check it, and I'd want that to be a nurse and not a manager.

say: I'd say **rules must come first**, because staff hear about new systems last.
I'd go to the **student union meeting** and share articles about nurses having a say.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy**: bedside care lasts, but paperwork goes first.
I fear saved time will be used to **cut posts**, not help patients.
do: Learn what the tools do by **watching a friend**, without typing my essays into one.
Join the student nurses' **workplace rights** group and borrow my mum's union handbook.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the ground moves but I can still stand.
S1.quote: I'd rather be slow and sure than the nurse who clicks accept on something wrong, because a wrong dose doesn't care how fast the software was.
fieldNote: She names **paperwork** as the part of nursing that goes first and care as the part that stays.
Her wariness of AI comes from **ward experience** through her mother, not abstract fear.
She turns worry into **joining a group**, which fits her union upbringing.

steps.text: Go to the student union meeting and join the student nurses' rights group
Watch a friend use an AI notes tool to understand what it does
Keep grades high and keep working Thursdays at the care home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules and that nobody should be sacked without a plan. I'd go online and be loud, which isn't like me. I'd also say to my lecturers that they need to tell us honestly what our degree is worth now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. Two years means I'm barely into second year, and hospitals would be rushing into this before anyone writes rules. I'd think my degree might be worth less than my parents paid for, and I'd feel guilty for even thinking that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd talk to my mum about which hands-on parts of nursing are safest, like theatre or mental health or community care. I'd keep studying because I don't know what else to do. I'd go to every protest and union event I could, and push the student union to demand a seat at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can picture the first year being chaotic: hospitals cutting posts, fast contracts, nobody knowing what the rules are. I wouldn't sleep much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What do you say to your parents the night you hear about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with them at the kitchen table and say we should talk about money, because my parents can pay for everything now but might not be able to in five years. I'd ask my dad, who's a teacher, whether his school is even expecting to exist in the same form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nursing is hands-on, why does that not reassure you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because thinking AI comes first, and robots follow around 2031. That gives hands-on nursing a few years of grace, but I'd graduate right into the part where the jobs are being redesigned. Hospitals are run by people with budgets, and budgets don't care how kind you are, so I'd want rules written before the first nurse is replaced.

say: I'd say we need **emergency rules** and no one sacked without a plan.
I'd tell lecturers to be **honest** about what our degree is worth.
think: I'd be **frightened**: hospitals would rush in before anyone writes rules.
I'd feel **guilty** for thinking my parents' money might be wasted.
do: Ask my mum which parts, like **theatre or community care**, look safest.
Go to every **union event** and push the student union for a seat at the table.
feel: **Alarmed**, expecting a chaotic first year and little sleep.
S2.quote: Hospitals are run by people with budgets, and budgets don't care how kind you are, so I'd want rules written before the first nurse is replaced.
fieldNote: Fear is mainly about **how fast hospital managers** would move, not about machines treating patients.
She mentions **guilt** about her parents' money, which she hadn't voiced earlier.
She would turn to **collective action** as an instinct.

steps.text: Ask my mum which nursing areas look safest in the first years
Attend every union event and push the student union for a seat at hospital talks
Write to my local politician demanding rules before any nurse is replaced
Sit down with my parents and talk honestly about money and plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still time to get the rules right, and we should use it. I'd talk to my course tutors about what the degree should teach in five years, like how to check software's work and how to talk to families. At the care home I'd chat to the staff to hear what they think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's survivable if the adults actually act. Five years means I graduate in about three and a half, and then have a year or two before the robots start entering wards. I'm worried they'll leave it to the last minute, though, because that's what they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in nursing and add things: a module on health data, maybe a placement in community care. I'd volunteer for the union's student branch and try to get a student nurse onto whatever committee talks about this. I'd save the money my part-time shifts bring in, even though my parents cover everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to breathe. I'd feel I had room to act, but also that everyone is guessing. I'd probably feel the weight of being one of the few students who actually reads about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time, compared with two years, actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me one thing: the chance to be better at the human side before the machines catch up. I could spend two years getting really good at the hardest conversations, like telling a family their mother is dying, because that is very hard to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change course, or stay in nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay. I considered public health, but nursing is what I actually want. If the thinking side of the job goes, the hands-on side and the kindness stay, and that's where I'd rather be. I'd just make sure I'm not the one left standing without a plan.

say: I'd say **there's time** to get the rules right and we should use it.
I'd ask tutors to teach us to **check software's work**.
think: Privately I think it's **survivable** if the adults act, but they usually leave it late.
I worry **everyone is guessing**, myself included.
do: Add a **health data module** and a community care placement to my degree.
Join the union's student branch and aim for a **committee seat**.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to breathe, with some room to act.
S3.quote: I could spend two years getting really good at the hardest conversations, like telling a family their mother is dying, because that is very hard to copy.
fieldNote: The longer warning shifts her toward **planning**, not complacency.
She keeps nursing as her goal and sees the **human side** as her edge.
She distrusts institutions to act **early**, which keeps her mood anxious.

steps.text: Take a health data module and add a community care placement
Join the union student branch and ask for a committee seat
Put my Saturday bookshop earnings into a savings account every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people stop pretending it's not coming. I'd argue for retraining funds, and for nurses to be paid more in the meantime, since the work will be changing. I'd say it at family dinners too, and my dad would roll his eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes me calmer, but I don't trust it. I'd be 29 by then, probably a ward nurse with a few years behind me, which is a better place to meet the change. I'd just worry that the ten years get wasted arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study as normal and aim for a specialist route, like palliative care, where people want a human. I'd start paying into a small pension early, which my mum keeps telling me to do. I'd also join a nurse's union as soon as I qualify, and take part in the talks about how the new software is introduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. It feels like having a long time to prepare for an exam I haven't seen the questions for. But I'd sleep fine, and I'd actually enjoy my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes about the way you'd study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less cramming, more depth. I'd take the electives that involve talking to patients and families, and read about how hospitals have handled change before. I'd stop worrying about getting every mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tech firms sell the dream and don't pay for the mess, and governments watch jobs vanish and say it's just the market. I'd also blame hospital bosses who'd cut staff the day they could. I don't blame ordinary people for using the tools, they're just trying to cope.

say: I'd say **ten years is plenty** if people stop pretending it isn't coming.
I'd argue for **retraining funds** and better pay for nurses now.
think: Privately I'm **calmer** but I don't trust the decade not to be wasted.
I'd like to meet the change as a **qualified ward nurse**, not a student.
do: Aim for a **specialist route** such as palliative care, where people want a human.
Start a small **pension** early and join a nurses' union on qualifying.
feel: **Uneasy** but sleeping fine, like waiting for an exam with unseen questions.
S4.quote: Tech firms sell the dream and don't pay for the mess, and governments watch jobs vanish and say it's just the market.
fieldNote: Her **blame** is clear and structural: tech firms, governments and hospital bosses.
She **doesn't blame ordinary users**, a sign of her compassion.
Ten years lets her plan a **specialism and pension**, so she moves from anxious to uneasy.

steps.text: Aim for a palliative care specialism after qualifying
Start a small pension contribution in my first year
Join a nurses' union on qualifying and join talks about new systems
Vote and campaign for retraining funds and better nurse pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, honestly, because I'd be in my second year with no time to find out what nursing even looks like afterwards. What would help is rules made early: hospitals can't swap nurses for software without asking staff, and people get paid properly while they retrain. I'd want those written down, not promised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't use AI tools at all, and people find that odd. I'd rather learn to read a frightened patient's face myself than trust a machine that has never sat on a hospital bed beside anyone. I'm not saying I'm right, I'm just slow to trust things that arrive with a lot of marketing.

headlineQuote: I'd rather learn to read a frightened patient's face myself than trust a machine that has never sat on a hospital bed beside anyone.
portrait: Maya is 19, in her first year of **nursing**, with a scholarship and a family that pays everything.
She is progressive and sceptical: she **never uses AI tools** and trusts unions and regulation more than companies.
Her stakes are the quality of care and whether nurses keep a say, more than her own paycheque.
She grows more worried as the warning time shrinks, and blames **tech firms and governments** for not setting rules early.
She leans on her nurse mother and her union habits, and would join a group rather than go it alone.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because she would have no time to see what nursing becomes.
whatWouldHelp: **Rules made early**, so hospitals need staff agreement before swapping nurses for software.
Proper **paid retraining** written into law, not promised in speeches.
